title: Women in the Colonies
objective: After this level you can explain coverture and the work colonial women did, from running households to growing indigo like Eliza Lucas Pinckney.
summary: Coverture merged a wife's legal identity into her husband's, but widows could run businesses. Eliza Lucas made indigo pay, with the labor and skill of enslaved people.

cards.headline: In colonial law, a married woman almost vanished.
cards.body: Under coverture she couldn’t even sign a contract. Yet women ran households, businesses and, in one case, a new industry.

cards.headline: Covered by her husband
cards.body: Colonists brought an English legal rule called coverture. A married woman’s legal existence merged into her husband’s: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name. On paper, a wife was covered by her husband, like a letter inside an envelope.

cards.headline: Women at work
cards.body: The law didn’t stop the work. Colonial households ran on women’s labor: cooking, cleaning, spinning, weaving, sewing, and making butter and soap. And unmarried women and widows, called femes soles, could own property, make contracts and run businesses in their own names. Lose a husband, gain a legal identity.

cards.headline: A teenager and a blue dye
cards.body: Around 1739 Eliza Lucas, 16, was left to manage her father’s Wappoo Plantation near Charleston and two larger South Carolina estates. After trying crops such as ginger and cotton, she grew a successful indigo crop. Indigo became South Carolina’s second most lucrative crop, after rice.

cards.headline: Whose hands?
cards.body: The story has more people in it. In colonial South Carolina, enslaved people did almost all the work of growing indigo and turning it into dye, skilled work learned through long experience. Lucas made the plans; their labor and know-how made the blue.

cards.headline: Women in the colonies: explained
learned: Coverture merged a wife’s legal identity into her husband’s
Widows and single women could own property and run businesses
Eliza Lucas, at 16, made indigo pay in South Carolina
Enslaved people’s labor and skill produced the indigo

questions.prompt: Under coverture, what could a married colonial woman not do?

options.label: Make contracts or sue in her own name

questions.explanation: Under coverture a wife’s legal existence merged into her husband’s.

questions.prompt: Why could a colonial widow run a business when a married woman usually could not?

options.label: As a feme sole she had a legal identity of her own
Her husband’s will required it
options.rationale: The rule applied to all femes soles.

options.label: Only widows could read
options.rationale: The difference was legal, not literacy.

questions.explanation: Unmarried women and widows, femes soles, could own property, make contracts and run businesses.

questions.prompt: Indigo became South Carolina’s second most lucrative crop. Which Level 13 crop of the Carolinas ranked first?

options.label: Wheat
options.rationale: That was the Middle Colonies’ grain.

options.label: Cotton
options.rationale: Lucas tried cotton, but rice led.

questions.explanation: Indigo was second only to rice, the other cash crop of the Carolinas.
